blocks.text: The musculoskeletal (MSK) examination assesses the bones, joints, muscles, tendons, ligaments and associated soft tissues to identify abnormalities affecting movement, stability, strength and function.

For OSCEs, your goal is to perform the examination systematically, demonstrate the correct techniques, recognise abnormal findings, interpret their clinical significance and present your findings confidently to the examiner.
This guide covers the general musculoskeletal examination, examination of individual joints, functional assessment, special tests, clinical interpretation and common viva questions.
1. General inspection
Posture, gait, deformities, muscle wasting, swelling, assistive devices and functional ability.
2. Joint examination
Look, feel, move (active and passive), measure where indicated, and perform special tests.
3. Range of motion and function
Movement, restriction, pain, stability, strength and functional limitations.
4. Special tests
Selected manoeuvres for ligament, tendon, meniscal, impingement and other pathology.
5. Completion and presentation
Neurovascular assessment, relevant adjacent joints, functional assessment and clinical summary.
The main examination principle is look, feel, move, followed by appropriate special tests and a neurovascular assessment.
For a painful joint, always examine the unaffected side first when appropriate, obtain consent, explain each manoeuvre and avoid forcing painful movements.

subsections.subsection_title: 4. The standard joint examination: Look, Feel, Move

blocks.text: This is the core of nearly every musculoskeletal OSCE.
Inspect both sides, comparing the affected joint with the opposite side.
Ask the patient whether the joint is painful before palpation. Begin away from the most painful area.

items.text: Temperature using the dorsum of your hand.
Tenderness over the joint line and surrounding structures.

blocks.text: Crepitus is a grating, crackling or crunching sensation during movement. It may occur in osteoarthritis, tendon disorders or other conditions; it is not specific to one diagnosis.
Assess both active and passive range of motion.

items.text: Active movement: The patient moves the joint independently.
Passive movement: The examiner moves the relaxed joint.
Resisted movement: The patient contracts the relevant muscles against resistance.

blocks.text: Interpretation:

rows: Active movement limited more than passive movement
Muscle weakness, tendon injury, pain inhibition or nerve dysfunction
Both active and passive movement restricted
Joint disease, capsular restriction, arthritis or mechanical obstruction

subsections.subsection_title: 5. Examination of the hands and wrists

blocks.text: Hand examination is particularly important in inflammatory arthritis, osteoarthritis, nerve compression and tendon disorders.
Ask the patient to place both hands palms down and then palms up.

items.text: Swelling of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP), proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints.
Swan-neck deformity: PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion.
Boutonnière deformity: PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension.
Dupuytren's contracture, which may cause flexion of the ring and little fingers.
Anatomical snuffbox if injury is suspected.

blocks.text: Assess warmth, tenderness, swelling and synovial thickening.

items.text: Rheumatoid arthritis often affects the MCP and PIP joints symmetrically.
Osteoarthritis commonly affects DIP and PIP joints and the first carpometacarpal joint.
Acute crystal arthritis may cause a very painful, hot and swollen joint.

blocks.text: These patterns overlap and should be interpreted with the history and investigations.

items.text: Touch the thumb to each fingertip.
Oppose the thumb to the little finger.
Perform radial and ulnar deviation of the wrists.

blocks.text: Assess grip strength and, where indicated, individual finger movements.
Phalen's test

Ask the patient to flex both wrists and hold the backs of the hands together for up to 60 seconds, if tolerated. Reproduction of tingling in the median nerve distribution supports carpal tunnel syndrome.
Tinel's sign
Gently tap over the median nerve at the wrist. Tingling in the median nerve distribution may support nerve irritation or compression.
Finkelstein-type manoeuvre

Gently position the thumb and wrist according to the chosen clinical technique. Pain over the radial styloid may suggest de Quervain tenosynovitis. Avoid forceful manoeuvres in an acutely painful wrist.
No single provocative test reliably establishes carpal tunnel syndrome. Interpret findings alongside the history, sensory distribution and, where indicated, nerve conduction studies.

blocks.title: Inspect the elbow from the front, sides and back for:

blocks.text: Assess temperature, tenderness and swelling.

items.text: Supinate the forearm, turning the palm upwards.
Pronate the forearm, turning the palm downwards.

blocks.text: Assess active and passive movements and then resisted movements where indicated.

items.text: Cozen's test: Resisted wrist extension may reproduce pain at the lateral epicondyle, supporting lateral epicondylalgia.
Medial epicondyle testing: Resisted wrist flexion or forearm pronation may reproduce pain in medial epicondylalgia.

blocks.text: These tests should be performed gently and interpreted with the location of tenderness and the patient's symptoms.
Shoulder examination is a common OSCE station because the joint has a wide range of motion and several potential sources of pain.
Expose both shoulders adequately and inspect from the front, side and back.
Identify focal tenderness and any swelling.
Assess:

rows: Often assessed by reaching behind the back

blocks.text: Ranges vary with technique and individual anatomy. Scapular movement contributes substantially to full shoulder elevation.
Ask the patient to perform active movement first, then assess passive movement if indicated.

items.text: Place a hand behind the head.
Reach behind the back towards the opposite shoulder blade.

blocks.text: These movements assess combined shoulder motion and can reveal functional limitations.
Neer's test
Stabilise the scapula and passively elevate the internally rotated arm. Reproduction of shoulder pain may support subacromial pain, but is not specific.
Hawkins–Kennedy test
Flex the shoulder and elbow to approximately 90°, then gently internally rotate the shoulder. Reproduction of pain may support subacromial pathology.
Empty-can test
Position the arms in the scapular plane with thumbs down and apply gentle downward resistance. Pain or weakness may indicate supraspinatus or related shoulder pathology.
Other tests include the painful arc, drop-arm test and external rotation strength testing. Select them according to the history and examination findings.

OSCE tip: Shoulder pain can arise from the cervical spine, rotator cuff, glenohumeral joint, acromioclavicular joint or other structures. Examine the neck and distal neurovascular status when appropriate.
Examine the cervical, thoracic and lumbar spine according to the patient's symptoms.
Palpate the spinous processes and paraspinal muscles for tenderness, deformity and muscle spasm.
If there is suspected fracture, major trauma or spinal instability, avoid provocative movements and follow appropriate spinal precautions.
Assess range, pain and movement quality.
This may be used to assess lumbar flexion, particularly in suspected axial spondyloarthritis.

items.text: Identify the lumbosacral region using the standard local technique.
Mark a measured segment of the lumbar spine, commonly 10 cm in total with 5 cm above and 5 cm below the lumbosacral landmark.
Ask the patient to bend forwards maximally.
Measure the change in distance between the marks.

blocks.text: Reduced expansion may indicate restricted lumbar flexion. The result depends on the technique used and is not diagnostic alone.

blocks.text: Red flags: New bladder or bowel dysfunction, saddle anaesthesia, progressive limb weakness, significant trauma, fever with spinal pain, or suspected malignancy or spinal infection require urgent assessment.
Hip disease can present with groin pain, thigh pain, buttock pain or referred knee pain.
Observe the patient walking, standing and lying supine where appropriate.

items.text: Anterior hip and groin region, as appropriate.

blocks.text: The hip joint is deep, so direct palpation of the joint itself is limited.
With the patient supine, assess:
Ranges vary by patient and measurement technique.
Technique

items.text: Flex the hip and knee to assess hip flexion.
Assess internal and external rotation with the hip and knee flexed.
Move the leg away from the midline for abduction.
Move it towards and across the midline for adduction.
Assess extension with an appropriate side-lying or prone technique if safe.

blocks.text: Painful or restricted internal rotation is a useful clue to hip joint pathology.
Thomas test
Used to assess a hip flexion contracture.

items.text: Ask the patient to lie supine.
Flex one hip and knee towards the chest to flatten the lumbar spine.

blocks.text: If the opposite thigh rises from the couch, a fixed flexion deformity may be present.
Trendelenburg test
Used to assess hip abductor function.

items.text: Stand behind the patient and ask them to stand on one leg, with support available if necessary.

blocks.text: A drop of the pelvis on the unsupported side suggests weakness or dysfunction of the stance-side hip abductors, although pain and other factors can affect the result.
FABER test (Patrick's test)
Flex the hip, abduct and externally rotate it, placing the ankle on the opposite knee. Gently lower the knee if tolerated.
Pain in the groin may suggest hip pathology; posterior pelvic pain may suggest sacroiliac-region pathology. The test is not specific enough to distinguish these conditions alone.
Log-roll test
Gently rotate the relaxed leg internally and externally while the patient lies supine. Pain or restricted movement may indicate hip joint pathology.
Do not force movement in suspected fracture or acute severe hip pain.
The knee is a common OSCE station involving assessment of effusion, ligament stability, meniscal pathology and degenerative disease.
Inspect the knees from the front, side and back.

items.text: Baker's cyst in the popliteal region.

blocks.text: Identify focal tenderness, warmth, swelling and crepitus.
**Bulge/sweep test**
Useful for a small knee effusion.

items.text: With the knee extended, gently sweep fluid upwards along the medial side of the knee.
Sweep downwards along the lateral side.
Observe for a fluid bulge on the medial side.

blocks.text: Useful for a larger effusion.

items.text: Milk fluid from the suprapatellar pouch towards the patella.
Gently press the patella posteriorly towards the femur.
A palpable tap or floating sensation may indicate fluid within the joint.

blocks.text: Do not perform these tests forcefully in a severely painful or acutely inflamed knee.

items.text: **In the normal knee joint** with minimal free fluid, the patella moves directly into the femoral condyle and there is no tapping sensation underneath the clinician’s fingertips.

**In the knee with excess fluid**, the patella is “floating” ; thus, ballottement causes the patella to tap directly against the femoral condyle. This sensation is transmitted to the clinician’s fingertips.

subsections.subsection_title: With patient supine, The knee and finger around patella while pushing any fluid from supra patellar pouch with other hand.

blocks.text: Fluctuation test is positive if finger and thumb are pushed apart.

The patient is supine and has knee in full extension. Starting at the medial tibiofemoral joint line, the examiner strokes upward two or three times toward the suprapatellar pouch in an attempt to move the swelling within the joint capsule to the suprapatellar pouch. The examiner then strokes downward on the distal lateral thigh, just superior to the suprapatellar pouch, toward the lateral joint line.
Stroke test is positive if fluid is observed on the medial side of the knee and quantified using a 5-point scale.
Examiner quickly pushes the patient’s patella posteriorly with two or three fingers. Positive if patella bounces off trochlea with a distinct impact.

This test is helpful in cases with very little fluid in the knee joint. After squeezing, any fluid out of the supra patellar pouch, the medial compartment of the joint is emptied by pressing on the inner aspect of the joint; that hand is then lifted away and the lateral side is sharply compressed to see a distinct ripple on the flattened medial surface as fluid is shunted across.

items.text: Passive range of motion where indicated.

blocks.text: Look for pain, restriction, crepitus and extensor mechanism dysfunction.
Lachman test — ACL
With the knee flexed approximately 20–30°, stabilise the femur and draw the tibia forwards. Excessive anterior translation or a soft endpoint compared with the other knee suggests ACL injury.
Posterior drawer — PCL
Flex the knee to approximately 90°, stabilise the foot and push the tibia backwards. Excessive posterior translation suggests PCL injury.
Valgus stress — MCL
Apply a controlled valgus force, testing at approximately 30° flexion and, when appropriate, in extension. Pain or excessive medial opening may indicate medial collateral ligament injury.
McMurray test — meniscus
Flex the knee and rotate the tibia while extending the knee using the appropriate medial or lateral manoeuvre. Joint-line pain or a palpable click may support meniscal pathology.

Additional tests include the anterior drawer test, posterior sag sign and Thessaly test. The Thessaly test requires weight-bearing and may be inappropriate in a patient with severe pain, instability or acute injury.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Examination of the ankle and foot

blocks.text: Inspect the feet and ankles from above, the sides and behind.

items.text: Charcot-type deformity in an appropriate clinical setting.

blocks.text: In patients with diabetes or suspected peripheral neuropathy, pay particular attention to skin integrity, ulcers, footwear and protective sensation.
Assess warmth, tenderness and swelling.
Test active movement first, followed by passive movement if appropriate.
Anterior drawer test of the ankle
Stabilise the distal tibia and draw the heel or talus forwards. Excessive translation compared with the opposite side may suggest anterior talofibular ligament injury.
Thompson test

items.text: Ask the patient to lie prone with the feet beyond the end of the couch, or position them appropriately.

blocks.text: Normal response is plantarflexion. Markedly reduced or absent plantarflexion raises concern for Achilles tendon rupture.
Ottawa ankle and foot rules

These are clinical decision rules used after acute ankle or midfoot injury to help determine whether radiographs are indicated. They incorporate specific areas of bony tenderness and the ability to bear weight. They do not replace clinical judgement and are intended for appropriate patient populations.
Beyond testing individual joints, assess functional movement and strength.
Ask the patient to rise from a chair, if safe.
If appropriate, ask the patient to squat and return to standing.
Observe knee alignment, hip mobility, balance and the ability to generate sufficient power.
Assess by asking the patient to squeeze two of your fingers or use a dynamometer if available.
Grip strength can help assess hand function, but it is influenced by pain, motivation, age and neurological status.
Ask the patient to stand or walk on their heels and toes if safe.
Weakness may indicate a neurological lesion, tendon dysfunction or other pathology.

blocks.title: For an injured or painful limb, document:

blocks.text: In an acutely injured limb, worsening pain, pain on passive stretch, tense swelling, paraesthesia or progressive weakness may indicate compartment syndrome or neurovascular compromise. These require urgent assessment.
These patterns are useful for clinical reasoning and OSCE viva questions.

rows: Activity-related pain, crepitus, restricted movement, bony enlargement and possible deformity
Symmetrical inflammatory synovitis, commonly involving MCP and PIP joints, with morning stiffness
Acute, severe pain with redness, warmth and swelling; commonly affects the first MTP joint
Acute painful, hot, swollen joint with marked pain on passive movement; fever may or may not be present
Painful shoulder movement, sometimes weakness on resisted movement
Median nerve distribution paraesthesia, possible thenar weakness or wasting
Instability following twisting trauma, sometimes with rapid swelling and a positive Lachman test
Joint-line pain, catching or locking, sometimes with an effusion
Sudden calf or heel pain, impaired push-off and abnormal Thompson test
Inflammatory back pain, reduced spinal mobility and sometimes restricted chest expansion
Symmetrical proximal weakness, such as difficulty climbing stairs or rising from a chair

blocks.text: Clinical patterns guide the differential diagnosis. Confirmation may require laboratory testing, imaging, aspiration or specialist assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: 14. How to present your findings to the examiner

blocks.text: A good presentation should be concise, structured and specific to the joint examined.
“On general inspection, the patient is comfortable at rest, with no obvious abnormal posture or gait disturbance.
On inspection of the affected joint, there is no obvious swelling, erythema, deformity, muscle wasting or surgical scar.
On palpation, the joint is not abnormally warm, and there is no focal tenderness or detectable effusion.
Active and passive ranges of motion are full and pain-free, with no significant crepitus. Power is preserved on resisted movements.
There is no demonstrable instability on the relevant special tests. Distal neurovascular status is intact.
In summary, the examination of the joint is unremarkable, with no obvious clinical evidence of significant structural or inflammatory pathology on the tests performed.”

For an abnormal examination, replace the normal findings with the precise location and nature of the abnormality. For example, document “warmth and effusion with marked pain on passive movement” rather than simply stating “abnormal knee examination.”
Do not report special tests, movements or neurovascular findings that you have not assessed.

Use this interactive checklist when practising with a colleague or simulated patient.
Introduce yourself, obtain consent and ask about pain
Inspect posture, gait and general function
Expose the relevant joint and compare both sides
Inspect for swelling, deformity, scars and muscle wasting
Palpate temperature, tenderness, landmarks and effusion
Assess active range of motion
Assess passive range of motion where indicated
Test resisted movement and muscle power
Perform appropriate joint-specific special tests
Assess adjacent joints when clinically indicated
Assess distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation and motor function when relevant
Assess gait and functional movement when safe
Thank the patient and restore comfort
Present findings and explain the likely clinical significance

Final exam tip: Master the general sequence first, then practise each joint separately. For every station, be able to describe what you see, explain what you feel, demonstrate the movements, interpret positive special tests and identify any urgent findings. In clinical practice, patient safety and a careful assessment are more important than completing every manoeuvre.

subsections.subsection_title: 17. The fundamental approach to an MSK examination

blocks.text: For a joint-focused examination, use:
Look → Feel → Move → Function → Special tests

blocks.title: For a broader musculoskeletal assessment, also consider:

blocks.text: A common screening tool is the GALS examination.
Observe walking, turning, balance, stride length and any limp or abnormal gait pattern.
Assess shoulder, elbow, wrist and hand function, including movement, grip and relevant deformities.
Assess hip, knee, ankle and foot movement, alignment and relevant functional tasks.
Inspect posture and spinal alignment, and assess movement when safe and indicated.
GALS is a screening examination, not a substitute for a detailed joint examination. Any abnormality should prompt a focused assessment.
Your report should cover the domains you actually assessed.
“The patient has a normal posture and gait, with no obvious musculoskeletal deformity or functional limitation.
There is no joint swelling, erythema, deformity or muscle wasting. The examined joints are not abnormally warm or tender, and there is no clinically detectable effusion.
Active and passive ranges of movement are full and pain-free. Muscle bulk and power are preserved, and there is no apparent joint instability on the tests performed.
The spine has no obvious abnormal curvature or focal tenderness. Distal neurovascular status is intact where assessed.
Overall, there are no significant abnormalities detected on the musculoskeletal examination performed.”
Important: Avoid claiming that every joint, ligament and neurovascular structure is normal if you performed only a screening examination.

subsections.subsection_title: 20. Distinguishable MSK conditions: features you must recognise

blocks.text: These are common clinical patterns that examiners expect you to distinguish.
Osteoarthritis (OA)

items.text: Morning stiffness is usually brief, often 30 minutes or less.
Bony enlargement and crepitus may be present.
Common sites include knees, hips, first carpometacarpal joints and distal interphalangeal joints.

blocks.text: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)

items.text: Inflammatory pain and prolonged morning stiffness.
Often affects MCP and PIP joints and wrists.
DIP joints are usually spared in classic RA.
Established disease may cause ulnar deviation, swan-neck and boutonnière deformities.

rows: May include fatigue and systemic inflammation

blocks.text: OSCE trap: Rheumatoid arthritis is not always symmetrical, and osteoarthritis can cause inflammatory flares. Use the complete clinical pattern rather than one feature alone.
Gout
Sudden, often overnight onset of severe pain, redness and swelling. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is a classic site, although other joints can be involved
Septic arthritis
An acutely painful, warm, swollen joint with markedly restricted movement. Fever may be present but can be absent. This is a potentially destructive emergency.

Critical distinction: Clinical appearance alone cannot reliably distinguish gout from septic arthritis. If infection is suspected, arrange urgent assessment and joint aspiration as appropriate. Crystals in synovial fluid do not exclude concurrent infection.

rows: Often around the joint line or joint itself
Often restricted or painful in significant joint disease

blocks.text: These distinctions are useful, but there is overlap. A tendon injury can restrict movement, and joint disease can cause pain during resisted movement.

content_groups.group_title: D. Meniscal versus ligament injury of the knee

blocks.text: Meniscal injury
Joint-line pain, swelling that may develop over hours, catching or locking, and symptoms after twisting on a weight-bearing knee.
Ligament injury
May cause instability or a feeling that the knee gives way. ACL injury may be associated with a twisting mechanism, a pop and rapid swelling from haemarthrosis.

items.text: Lachman test: Assesses anterior translation of the tibia and is particularly useful for ACL injury.
Anterior drawer test: Also assesses ACL integrity.
Posterior drawer test: Assesses PCL integrity.
Varus and valgus stress tests: Assess lateral and medial collateral ligament stability, respectively.
McMurray test: May support a diagnosis of meniscal pathology.

blocks.text: No single test is perfect, and acute pain or swelling can reduce the reliability of examination.

Weakness and pain with shoulder elevation or resisted movements; passive movement may be relatively preserved
Median nerve symptoms, often affecting the thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger
Pain around the radial wrist near the first dorsal compartment, often provoked by thumb movement
Localised tendon pain and tenderness, commonly aggravated by loading
Heel pain, often worse with the first steps after rest
Chronic back pain beginning at a younger age, improvement with exercise, and prolonged morning stiffness may suggest inflammatory disease
Localised inflamed swelling over a bursa; infection must be considered, particularly with fever or skin breakdown

subsections.subsection_title: 21. Common “Why did you do that?” OSCE questions

blocks.text: The examiner wants to know the clinical purpose of your action. Answer with the structure: what you are assessing, why it matters, and what an abnormal result may suggest.

rows: Why do you observe the patient walking?
To assess gait, weight-bearing, balance, joint function and possible pain-related limitation.
Why do you compare both sides?
To identify asymmetry in swelling, deformity, muscle bulk, movement or strength.
Why do you inspect before palpation?
To identify visible abnormalities and establish a baseline before touching the patient.
Why do you examine the joint above and below?
Pathology in adjacent joints can contribute to symptoms, and pain may be referred from another site.
To determine how the abnormality affects everyday activities and mobility.
To identify local warmth that may indicate inflammation, infection or recent injury.
Why do you palpate the joint line?
To assess for focal tenderness that may indicate intra-articular pathology, such as meniscal injury in the knee.
Why do you assess for effusion?
To determine whether fluid is present within the joint, which may occur with inflammation, trauma or infection.
Why do you look for muscle wasting?
It may indicate chronic disuse, pain inhibition, denervation or muscle disease.
It may indicate irregular joint surfaces or other movement-related abnormalities, although it is not specific to OA.
Why do you assess active movement first?
It assesses the patient's own functional movement and helps identify pain or weakness before the examiner moves the joint.
Why do you assess passive movement?
It helps distinguish active movement limitation from restriction involving the joint, capsule or other structures.
Why do you test power against resistance?
To quantify muscle strength and assess relevant muscle-tendon units and neurological function.
To identify abnormal ligamentous laxity or joint instability.
Why do you use a goniometer?
To measure joint range of motion more objectively and monitor changes over time.
Why do you perform the Lachman test?
To assess anterior tibial translation and the integrity of the ACL.
Why do you perform the McMurray test?
To look for symptoms or signs consistent with meniscal pathology.
Why do you perform the Trendelenburg test?
To assess pelvic control during single-leg stance, particularly hip abductor function.
Why do you perform the Thomas test?
To assess for a hip flexion contracture.
Why do you perform Phalen's test?
To see whether sustained wrist flexion reproduces symptoms suggestive of median nerve compression at the carpal tunnel.
Why do you perform the Finkelstein test?
To reproduce pain associated with first dorsal compartment pathology, including De Quervain tenosynovitis; technique matters because related manoeuvres can be confused.

blocks.text: Safety answer to remember: If an examination manoeuvre would cause unnecessary pain or risk worsening an injury, you should modify or omit it and explain why.
Look → Feel → Move → Function

items.text: Look: Swelling, deformity, scars and muscle wasting.
Feel: Temperature, tenderness, effusion and bony landmarks.
Move: Active and passive range of motion.
Function: Strength, stability and relevant activities.

blocks.text: Add special tests when indicated.
**“Rest stiff, movement helps”**
Inflammatory arthritis commonly causes prolonged morning stiffness and stiffness after inactivity, often improving with movement. Mechanical pain commonly worsens with loading or activity.
This is a guide rather than a rule: inflammatory disease can hurt with activity, and advanced OA may cause pain at rest or at night.
**“Swan up, bouton down”**

items.text: Swan-neck: PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion.
Boutonnière: PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension.

blocks.text: These patterns help distinguish characteristic deformities in established rheumatoid arthritis and other connective tissue or tendon disorders.
**“None, flicker, slide, lift, resist, normal”**
Always state which muscle group you tested and whether pain limited the effort.
**“Lachman forward, drawer back”**

items.text: Lachman: Anterior tibial translation; assesses the ACL.
Anterior drawer: Also assesses the ACL.
Posterior drawer: Posterior tibial translation; assesses the PCL.
Varus stress: Assesses the lateral collateral ligament complex.
Valgus stress: Assesses the medial collateral ligament complex.

blocks.text: Interpret laxity in relation to the opposite knee and the quality of the endpoint.
**“Trendelenburg = pelvic control”**

During single-leg stance, the pelvis should remain approximately level. A drop on the unsupported side suggests impaired stance-side hip abductor function, although pain and other factors can also produce an abnormal result.

rows: Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, internal and external rotation
Flexion, extension, radial and ulnar deviation
Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and thumb opposition
Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, internal and external rotation
Dorsiflexion, plantar flexion, inversion and eversion
Flexion, extension, lateral flexion and rotation, as appropriate

blocks.text: Exam tip: Demonstrate each movement yourself before asking the patient to perform it. This improves understanding and helps the patient avoid unnecessary discomfort.

subsections.subsection_title: 24. MSK viva questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the difference between arthralgia and arthritis?
Answer: Arthralgia means joint pain without necessarily having objective inflammation. Arthritis refers to inflammation of a joint, often producing swelling, warmth, pain and restricted movement.
Q2. What is synovitis?
Answer: Inflammation of the synovial membrane, which can produce soft joint swelling, warmth, pain and restricted movement.
Q3. What is the difference between a joint effusion and synovial thickening?
Answer: An effusion is excess fluid within the joint cavity. Synovial thickening reflects hypertrophy or inflammation of the synovial tissue. They may coexist.
Q4. What is crepitus?
Answer: A grating, crackling or clicking sensation or sound during movement. It can occur in OA but is not specific to that condition.
Q5. What is a contracture?
Answer: A persistent restriction of movement caused by shortening or tightening of soft tissues around a joint, or by other structural changes.
Q6. Why should you examine adjacent joints?
Answer: Pain can be referred from another joint, and abnormalities in one joint can alter the biomechanics and function of neighbouring joints.
Q7. Which joints are commonly affected in rheumatoid arthritis?
Answer: The wrists, MCP and PIP joints are commonly affected. The disease often produces symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis. DIP joints are usually spared in the classic pattern.
Q8. What are Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes?
Answer: Heberden's nodes are bony enlargements at the DIP joints. Bouchard's nodes occur at the PIP joints. They are classically associated with hand OA.
Q9. How can gout be confirmed?
Answer: Identification of monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid is the diagnostic gold standard when aspiration is feasible. Serum urate alone neither confirms nor excludes acute gout.
Q10. Why is septic arthritis an emergency?

Answer: Infection can rapidly destroy cartilage and cause systemic illness. Urgent assessment, synovial fluid sampling and appropriate antimicrobial treatment are required; drainage may also be necessary.
Q11. What is the difference between rheumatoid arthritis and OA on palpation?
Answer: RA commonly produces soft, boggy synovial swelling and warmth. OA often produces hard bony enlargement, although effusion and inflammatory changes can occur during OA flares.

content_groups.group_title: C. Shoulder, hip and knee viva

blocks.text: Q12. What is a painful arc at the shoulder?
Answer: Pain during a portion of active shoulder abduction, classically around 60–120 degrees. It may occur with subacromial pain, but is not specific to one diagnosis.
Q13. How do you distinguish adhesive capsulitis from a rotator cuff problem?

Answer: Adhesive capsulitis typically restricts both active and passive movement, particularly external rotation. Rotator cuff pathology often causes pain or weakness with active or resisted movement while passive range may be relatively preserved.
Q14. What does a positive Trendelenburg test indicate?

Answer: A drop of the unsupported side of the pelvis during single-leg stance suggests impaired hip abductor function on the stance side. Pain, weakness and other balance problems can also affect the test.
Q15. What is the purpose of the Lachman test?
Answer: It assesses anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur and is used to evaluate ACL injury.
Q16. What is a locked knee?

Answer: A true locked knee has a mechanical block preventing full extension. A displaced meniscal tear or loose body is among the possible causes. A painful knee that the patient is reluctant to move is not necessarily mechanically locked.

subsections.subsection_title: 25. Clinical presentations: how to summarise common cases

blocks.text: Model presentation

“There is bony enlargement of the knee with crepitus, reduced range of movement and pain on movement. There is no marked erythema or acute inflammatory change. These findings are consistent with a degenerative joint process, such as knee osteoarthritis, in the appropriate clinical context.”

content_groups.group_title: Case 2: Rheumatoid arthritis of the hands

blocks.text: Model presentation

“There is symmetrical soft swelling and tenderness of the MCP and PIP joints, with restricted movement and established hand deformities. The pattern is suggestive of inflammatory polyarthritis, including rheumatoid arthritis. I would correlate the findings with the history, systemic examination and appropriate investigations.”
Model presentation

“The knee is acutely swollen, warm and severely tender, with marked restriction of active and passive movement. Septic arthritis must be excluded urgently. I would arrange immediate clinical assessment and joint aspiration as appropriate.”
Model presentation

“The patient reports a twisting injury followed by knee swelling and instability. There is increased anterior tibial translation on Lachman testing compared with the contralateral knee. These findings raise suspicion of ACL injury, and further assessment and imaging may be required.”
Model presentation

“There is painful restriction of both active and passive shoulder movement, particularly external rotation. This pattern is suggestive of adhesive capsulitis, subject to the history and exclusion of other causes of shoulder stiffness.”

items.text: Hot, acutely swollen joint: Consider septic arthritis and arrange urgent assessment.
Significant trauma with deformity or inability to bear weight: Consider fracture or dislocation.
Acute limb pain with neurovascular compromise: Requires emergency assessment.
Progressive weakness or sensory deficit: Consider neurological compression or another serious cause.
Back pain with new bladder dysfunction, saddle sensory loss or progressive weakness: Consider cauda equina syndrome and arrange emergency assessment.
Unexplained persistent bone pain, mass or pathological fracture: Consider malignancy or another serious bone disorder.
Systemic illness with joint pain: Consider infection or systemic inflammatory disease.

Try answering these aloud before checking the answers.
1. A patient has bony DIP enlargement and brief morning stiffness. What is the likely diagnosis?
A. Rheumatoid arthritis
B. Osteoarthritis
C. Septic arthritis
D. Gout
2. A patient has a hot, swollen knee and fever. What is your priority?
A. Perform all ligament tests
B. Arrange routine physiotherapy
C. Urgently assess for septic arthritis
D. Prescribe exercise without further assessment
3. Both active and passive shoulder movements are restricted, especially external rotation. What is suggested?
A. Isolated rotator cuff weakness
B. Adhesive capsulitis
C. Carpal tunnel syndrome
D. ACL injury
4. Which test assesses the ACL?
A. Posterior drawer
B. Lachman
C. Trendelenburg
D. Phalen
5. What does a positive Trendelenburg test suggest?
A. Hip abductor dysfunction
B. A meniscal tear
C. Median nerve compression
D. An ankle ligament tear

The principle to remember: In every MSK OSCE, describe the abnormality before naming the diagnosis. State the location, side, tenderness, movement restriction and relevant special-test findings, then explain what they suggest. Always consider septic arthritis, significant trauma and neurovascular compromise when the clinical presentation warrants it.
